reports.name: Junior Caminero
reports.published_report: The 44-home-run projection isn't the headline — the Statcast profile underneath it is. At 93.0 mph average exit velocity and 50.8% hard-hit rate, Caminero is one of the most forceful contact makers in Tampa's lineup, and an .xSLG of .502 says the raw power translates without much luck attached. What makes the profile unusual at 23 is the 12.4% walk rate sitting alongside it, genuinely elite discipline for a hitter who barrels the ball that often. The one flag is defense: a 1st-percentile OAA reading is hard to ignore, and if Tampa eventually moves him off third base, the profile shifts from impact corner to DH-dependent slugger.

reports.name: James Wood
reports.published_report: The contact-and-discipline side of this profile is almost absurdly clean for a 23-year-old: a 22.3% chase rate paired with 16.7% walks, and when he connects the ball leaves at 95.1 mph average exit velocity with a 22.0% barrel rate that both grade at the top of the scale. The problem is the 29.2% strikeout rate, which sits near the bottom of the league, and whether he can hold that chase discipline under a full season of pressure is the one thing the entire profile hinges on. If pitchers find a way to expand that whiff rate, which is already at 31.4%, the batting average bleeds and the .425 xwOBA starts looking like a ceiling rather than a floor. But if the plate discipline holds, the power production is broad enough and the walk rate high enough that a .387 OBP with 41-homer pop is not a reach.

reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: The .405 xwOBA and 2.73 xERA living in the same Statcast card is the whole argument: he's a genuine top-tier threat on both sides of the ball simultaneously. As a hitter, the 16.4% barrel rate and 13.9% walk rate anchor a profile that projects to .279/.385/.533, and the 30.2% whiff rate is the one real cost, a swing-and-miss tendency that sits well below average but hasn't stopped him from being one of the most dangerous bats in the lineup. On the mound, a 98.1 mph fastball paired with a 2488 rpm spin rate produces a 27.9% strikeout rate and suppresses hard contact to a 3.8% barrel rate allowed, which is why the xERA lands where it does. The whole thing hinges on health, specifically whether the Dodgers deploy him as a two-way player consistently enough that both profiles stay sharp, because a version where the pitching workload gets managed down to a handful of starts is a version where that mound upside quietly evaporates.

reports.published_report: The xSLG of .474 with an 11.5% barrel rate is doing something interesting: it's outrunning the average exit velocity and hard-hit numbers that would normally generate it, which means Abrams is getting to his damage efficiently rather than through sheer brute force. The .354 xwOBA puts him well above the middle of the league, and the projection translating that into a .529 SLG over 666 plate appearances reflects a hitter who has figured out how to make contact matter. Langford's Statcast profile reads like a league-average bat with a speed bonus: his xwOBA and xBA both sit right at the median, his xSLG at .438 shows some real pop, but a 5.6% walk rate dragging in the 14th percentile flattens everything downstream. The projection at .270/.333/.487 across 456 PA is essentially saying the legs at 28.5 ft/s and barrel rate keep him afloat, and 14 stolen bases at that sprint speed is a reasonable floor for the running game's contribution. If the walk rate stays buried, he's a useful second-division regular; if he learns to take a pitch, the projected .487 SLG and that speed give you a genuine everyday player worth building around.

reports.name: Jesús Made
reports.published_report: The contact is the whole argument. At 19 years old in Double-A, Jesús Made is striking out in just 15% of his plate appearances across 389 PA, and the MLB-equivalent translation puts that at 18.6% — a rate that would play comfortably in a big-league lineup where most hitters run well north of that. The power is still forming, with a .160 ISO at AA that translates to .131, so the ceiling hinges on whether he develops even average pull-side thump as he fills out physically. If it comes, he's a low-end everyday shortstop; if the bat stays this clean but the power plateaus, he's a useful regular who earns his spot on discipline and 29 stolen bases rather than thump.

reports.name: Xavier Edwards
reports.published_report: The contact-and-discipline profile is genuinely elite: 13.7% strikeout rate, 11.5% walk rate, a 16.4% whiff rate that most leadoff hitters would envy. The Statcast batting average estimator (.263 xBA) suggests he'll keep hitting for average even when results don't fully cooperate, but 87.0 mph average exit velo and a 28.8% hard-hit rate are bottom-of-the-barrel power indicators, and the .318 xwOBA reflects that ceiling plainly. The projection (.287/.364/.394) is essentially what the Statcast card draws up: a high-OBP, low-slug middle infielder whose value lives in contact rate, plate discipline, and 25 projected stolen bases. The whole thing collapses if he loses the walk or the bat-to-ball, because there's no power cushion underneath.

reports.name: Daylen Lile
reports.published_report: The sprint speed is legitimate, 29.3 ft/s in the 94th percentile, and the projection's 15 stolen bases reflect it. Everything else in the Statcast profile is the tension: a 37.8% chase rate in the bottom 11th percentile of the zone, paired with a 5.9% walk rate that trails most of the league, means the hit tool has to do more work than it probably can. The .313 xwOBA sitting at the 42nd percentile while xBA and xSLG read closer to league average tells you the batted-ball quality isn't making up for the plate discipline gap. reports.name: Gabriel Moreno
reports.published_report: The xBA sits at .302, 98th percentile, and that's not a profile propped up by soft contact finding holes. His 16.1% whiff rate and 12.0% walk rate both land in the upper eighties and low nineties percentile-wise, and together they describe a catcher who makes better contact decisions than almost anyone in the league. The power is modest by Statcast standards, a 7.7% barrel rate that lands right at the median, but the .380 xwOBA says he doesn't need to barrel everything to produce. If the projection's .301/.383/.442 line holds across 496 plate appearances, he's one of the most complete offensive catchers in baseball, and the Statcast profile gives you every reason to believe it does.

reports.name: Logan Webb
reports.published_report: The gap between a 4.04 xERA and a projected 3.79 ERA is the whole profile in miniature. Webb doesn't miss bats, his 20.6% whiff rate sits in the 13th percentile, but his 34.2% chase rate is in the 85th percentile and hitters who expand the zone get barrels on only 5.6% of their contact. He wins on location and weak contact, not swing-and-miss, and that formula holds as long as command stays tight: his 6.3% walk rate is an asset, and the day it slips is the day the xERA catches the ERA. Figure a mid-rotation grinder who posts 18 quality starts, doesn't embarrass you in October, and gives you nothing extra.

reports.name: Royce Lewis
reports.published_report: The barrel rate is the loudest thing in this profile. At 11.6%, it sits in the 77th percentile, and it's attached to a hitter whose average exit velocity and hard-hit rate are both exactly league average, which means he's making contact that matters when he makes it. The problem is the 34.0% whiff rate, seventh percentile, and it drags everything downstream: an xBA of .219, an xwOBA of .301, and a projection sitting at .222/.299/.397 across 483 PA that reads like a guy perpetually one hot week away from looking useful and one cold stretch away from the lineup card. His 10.2% walk rate keeps the floor from caving in entirely, but this profile hinges on whether the strikeout problem is injury-related variance or just who he is at the plate now.

reports.name: Jesús Luzardo
reports.published_report: The xERA sits at 2.86 and the strikeout rate is 29.9%, and together they describe a frontline starter whose underlying numbers have quietly outrun his reputation. Luzardo misses bats at a 31.8% whiff rate and keeps barrels down to 5.5%, so the contact he does allow lands soft, with average exit velocity at 86.8 mph. The one real wrinkle is the walk rate at 7.5%, which sits well below his other markers and is the profile's pressure valve: if command tightens even a little, a 3.31 ERA projection over 186 innings starts to look conservative rather than optimistic. A true number-two starter who could pitch like a number one if the walks behave.

reports.name: Eury Pérez
reports.published_report: The fastball spins at 2669 rpm, 99th percentile, and sits 98.2 mph. That's the reason to believe in Eury Pérez. The problem is that a 9.5% walk rate is bleeding the strikeout rate dry — 26.6% punchouts sound useful until you notice the barrel rate is 10.9%, meaning when hitters do connect, they connect well, and the xERA sits at 4.01 despite the swing-and-miss stuff. The projection at 3.70 ERA over 150.6 innings is the optimistic read: it assumes the stuff-to-command gap closes enough that the 27.8% whiff rate and 32.2% chase rate carry more innings than the walks surrender. If the walk rate stays at 9.5%, what's left is a starter with a great fastball who never quite puts it together.

reports.name: Shane McClanahan
reports.published_report: The ERA from his last healthy season made McClanahan look like a budding ace, but the Statcast profile from his most recent sample tells a more complicated story. His xERA sits at 4.16 with a 22.2% strikeout rate, both right at the middle of the league, which means the 3.35 ERA projection is leaning hard on contact management and a whiff-and-chase combination that has some real teeth: 27.0% whiff rate, 32.0% chase rate, both above average. The profile holds if he can keep limiting barrels, where his 8.8% barrel rate and 39.7% hard-hit rate suggest some exposure, and if his Tommy John recovery delivers a fastball that actually plays at 95.6 mph rather than just registering it. If the stuff doesn't sharpen, what's left is a rotation arm who lives on the margins of hitter mistakes.

reports.name: Bryson Stott
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here is quieter than the counting stats suggest. His xwOBA sits at .320, right at the league median, and his hard-hit rate of 38.3% and average exit velocity of 89.1 mph both trail a majority of hitters, so the projection's 12 home runs and .405 slugging aren't built on loud contact. What keeps the floor from caving in is a 19.7% whiff rate that grades out well, an 18.7% strikeout rate that won't bleed away at-bats, and sprint speed at 28.5 ft/s — fast enough to make 25 projected steals credible and to pull the xBA up to .264 on balls that wouldn't hurt a slower runner. The whole profile hinges on that speed staying functional; if he loses a step, the average-exit-velo problem has nowhere to hide and you're left with a league-median bat at second base with a 7.2% walk rate. Right now he's a useful, limited second-division regular.

reports.name: Hunter Brown
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here is essentially two pitchers stitched together. Brown's 29.4% whiff rate and 86.6 mph average exit velocity tell you the stuff plays, because hitters who make contact aren't doing much with it, but a 14.0% walk rate undercuts almost everything else, sitting at the fourth percentile among starters and dragging a legitimate swing-and-miss arsenal toward a 3.69 xERA rather than something meaningfully better. The 26.2% chase rate explains the walks: batters aren't chasing, so he's either pounding the zone and getting whiffs in it, or falling behind and gifting free passes. If the command stabilizes even to league-average territory, the barrel suppression and whiff rate combine into a mid-rotation anchor; if the walks stay where they are, 107.1 projected innings and a 3.57 ERA describes a guy Houston keeps running out there because the ceiling keeps teasing them.

reports.name: Mickey Moniak
reports.published_report: The .518 projection SLG tells you almost everything, but the Statcast profile underneath it shows a gap that matters. His barrel rate (10.9%) and hard-hit rate (43.4%) are legitimately above average, and the projection's .831 OPS leans into that contact quality, yet his xBA sits at .225 and his xwOBA at .301, both well below his actual production, because a 41.9% chase rate that ranks near the bottom of the league keeps turning at-bats into nothing before the good swing ever arrives. He can run into 23 home runs in 418 plate appearances if enough of those hard swings find air — the power shape is real enough to support the .518 SLG at Coors, and sprint speed at 28.3 ft/s means he earns a few extra hits. But if the chase rate stays where Statcast has it, you're looking at a corner outfielder whose walk rate (5.5%) can't carry the strikeout rate (24.7%), and the .831 OPS becomes optimistic reliance on park.

Schanuel's .285 xBA sits in genuinely elite company for contact quality, but his 2.6% barrel rate and 87.2 mph average exit velocity say the ball doesn't travel — he finds gaps and barrels that aren't barrels, so the .383 xSLG lands in the bottom half of the league. If the contact profile holds and he sneaks into a lineup spot where on-base percentage is currency, he's a useful everyday first baseman; if the power floor doesn't nudge upward as he fills out at 24, he becomes a tough platoon sell at a premium offensive position.

reports.name: Dustin May

A 3.98 xERA sitting comfortably above league average, a 7.5% walk rate that outperforms most starters, 96.9 mph on the fastball — the building blocks look real. Then the 46.1% hard-hit rate and 90.2 mph average exit velocity arrive and explain why the ERA projection lands at 4.39 instead of matching the xERA: batters are squaring him up at a rate that contact management alone can't fix, and a 22.8% whiff rate doesn't generate enough empty swings to bail him out when command slips. The whole thing hinges on whether the barrel suppression (6.1%) can keep limiting the damage that the hard-hit rate keeps threatening, because if barrels start converting at a harder clip over a full season, 167.4 innings of this profile is a back-end starter grinding through contact. He's a number four who looks like a number three on the good days and reminds you why he isn't on the bad ones.

reports.name: Michael Soroka
reports.published_report: The walk rate carries this profile. At 5.1%, Soroka sits comfortably ahead of most starters in limiting free passes, and that control keeps him functional even when the swing-and-miss isn't there, because the 22.2% whiff rate is below average and doesn't figure to bail him out on its own. What makes the contact picture livable is his 33.6% chase rate, which nudges hitters into weak decisions without requiring dominant stuff, and the 87.7 mph average exit velocity suggests he's managing damage reasonably well despite the modest 93.7 mph fastball. reports.name: Luke Keaschall
reports.published_report: The contact and discipline profile is genuinely elite; the power is not. Keaschall's 22.6% chase rate and 17.1% whiff rate both rank near the top of the league, and he draws walks at a 10.3% clip, but his 84.6 mph average exit velocity sits at the 2nd percentile — the bat-to-ball ability shows up everywhere in the plate-discipline numbers, and nowhere in the damage. The projection reflects exactly that tension: a .258/.351/.352 line across 559 PA, where the .351 OBP does the heavy lifting and the .352 slugging tells you the seven projected home runs aren't an accident of suppression. Add 19 stolen bases from a 28.8 ft/s sprint, and what you have is a second baseman whose value runs entirely through on-base and legs, with the floor being a useful bench piece and the ceiling a low-end regular if he keeps beating contact metrics that his exit velocity says he shouldn't be able to sustain.

reports.name: Cade Cavalli
reports.published_report: The fastball at 96.7 mph is loud, but the Statcast profile underneath it is a study in contradictions. His K% at 26.6% is genuine production, and a 7.1% walk rate shows he can command it well enough to let the stuff play — yet his Whiff% and Chase% both sit right at league average, which means hitters aren't chasing and aren't flailing, they're just making contact on pitches that happen to miss barrels. That 6.6% Barrel% is encouraging, but the whole read on Cavalli hinges on whether the strikeouts hold without the swing-and-miss numbers to explain them. If the profile stabilizes, you get something close to the 3.59 ERA projection, a solid mid-rotation piece who beats contact rather than avoids it; if the strikeouts regress toward the whiff rate, what's left is a 96.7 mph arm with average movement and a 3.96 xERA ceiling.

reports.name: Connor Prielipp
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is doing real work here, but the whiff numbers don't back it up the way you'd want. Prielipp sits 95.5 mph and punches out 24.4% of hitters, yet his 22.7% whiff rate lands in the 29th percentile, which means those strikeouts are leaning heavily on called strikes and contact mis-hits rather than genuine swing-and-miss. The contact quality tells the same uncomfortable story: 40.7% hard-hit rate, 8.9% barrel rate, average exit velocity at 90.3 mph, all bottom third, and a 4.04 xERA that matches the .310 xwOBA in suggesting a pitcher who's roughly league-average once the dust settles. He's a back-of-the-rotation starter if the command tightens enough to keep that 8.3% walk rate from compounding the contact issues, and a depth arm if it doesn't — the projection's 4.40 ERA over 120.9 innings is the honest ceiling, not the floor to build from.

His 13.6% strikeout rate and 13.0% walk rate are both near the top of the percentile card, and the xwOBA of .348 says the underlying contact quality is real enough to support the projection's .342 OBP even without a power spike. The 6.2% barrel rate is the quiet limitation, keeping him off the elite slugger tier and explaining why the projection lands at 19 home runs rather than 30, but 37 projected stolen bases at 33 says the legs are still part of the profile. The 28.9% whiff rate is the load-bearing problem: he generates real damage when he squares it up, but he misses enough to drag xBA down to .246 and leave the full offensive line looking like a .214/.291/.371 projection across 561 PA. Add 29.2 ft/s sprint speed at the 93rd percentile plus a 92nd-percentile OAA mark in the outfield, and the path to a regular role runs entirely through whether he can tighten the contact quality — if the whiff rate doesn't improve, he's a plus defender with pop who plays himself into a platoon.

reports.name: Chad Patrick

reports.name: Spencer Torkelson
reports.published_report: The tension in Torkelson's profile is almost perfectly drawn: a 14.1% barrel rate sitting near the top of the league, a 23.0% chase rate that would make most contact hitters jealous, and a 32.3% strikeout rate that is quietly one of the worst marks you'll find on a full-time player. He sees pitches well enough to barrel them, then whiffs at 31.4% once he swings — the chase discipline and the swing-and-miss live in completely different bodies. The xBA of .215 is not a rounding error; pitchers have learned to expand the zone after the first strike and he has no answer, which is why a .318 xwOBA translates to a projected .213 AVG and a .723 OPS across 622 PA. If the strikeout rate ever bends toward something livable, there's a 28-homer, above-average walk rate regular here; if it doesn't, he's a first baseman hitting .213 with good power who costs you a lineup spot every time he bats.

Eldridge's average exit velocity of 92.4 mph sits at the 91st percentile, and his .365 xwOBA reflects genuine contact quality, not a BABIP run, because the walk rate of 13.8% keeps the on-base floor honest even when the strikeouts climb to 26.2%. The projection's .779 OPS across 420 PA undersells the underlying Statcast shape, and if the strikeout rate comes down even modestly, a .485 xSLG becomes a real-world number rather than an expected one. The whole thing hinges on whether the plate discipline that produced that walk rate can suppress the strikeouts enough to let the raw power translate, because at a corner-only profile, a 26.2% K rate without improvement leaves you with a useful but capped first baseman rather than a middle-of-the-order piece.

reports.name: Bryan Baker
reports.published_report: The xERA sitting at 2.69 and an xwOBA of .255 both land in the 95th percentile, and neither number is doing the other's job — they're describing the same pitcher from two different angles, and the picture is consistent. Baker's 35.8% chase rate is the engine: hitters expanding off the zone drives the 29.1% whiff rate and keeps the hard contact down to 32.7%, well below what most relievers allow. The walk rate at 8.4% is the one thing keeping this from being a cleaner profile, sitting right at league average and the only number in the card that doesn't confirm the rest. If that holds at its current level, the projection's 2.33 ERA and 39 saves are what a full season of this looks like for Tampa Bay's closer; if the control drifts, the chase rate can't absorb a meaningful BB% climb at the back of a bullpen.

reports.name: Gage Jump
reports.published_report: The fastball is loud, 96.3 mph with 2355 rpm spin, and hitters are chasing at 31.7%, but the barrel rate and hard-hit numbers tell a different story: a 43.1% hard-hit rate and 90.3 mph average exit velocity that sits near the bottom of the league. Jump's K% of 24.9% is solid enough to project 116 strikeouts across 113.2 innings, yet the whiff rate of 23.6% doesn't match what the velo and spin suggest it should be, which means the chase is doing a lot of the heavy lifting right now. If hitters adjust their two-strike approach and stop expanding, the xERA of 4.24 is probably the floor, not the ceiling, and the projected 1.4 WHIP reflects a guy who needs cleaner sequencing to survive in a rotation. The profile is a backend starter who could hold a job, as long as that chase rate isn't something hitters learn to ignore.

His xSLG sits at .431 with a 43.9% hard-hit rate, but his xBA is .240 and his 29.8% whiff rate is below-average — he's hitting the ball hard when he hits it, and missing too often when he doesn't. The sprint speed at 29.3 ft/s is elite and keeps the floor from caving, turning singles into problems for defenses and soft contact into hits that don't show up in expected stats. If the swing-and-miss tightens, the power translates into something real; if it doesn't, the projection's .692 OPS is probably the ceiling rather than a conservative floor, and he settles into a second-division regular who runs well and doesn't hurt you.

reports.name: Logan Henderson
reports.published_report: A 31.8% strikeout rate paired with a 4.7% walk rate, both sitting at the 96th percentile, is the kind of command-to-stuff combination that makes a 2.88 xERA feel honest rather than lucky. The fastball sits 93.0 mph, below-average velocity for a starter, so the strikeouts are coming from sequencing and spin (2361 rpm on the fastball) rather than pure heat, and that fragility matters because the chase rate is just 29.7%, meaning hitters aren't expanding much out of the zone. The projection calls for a 3.51 ERA over 84.2 innings, which is what you'd expect when a real underlying skill profile gets slightly nicked by contact that doesn't always behave, given that his 8.6% barrel rate sits in the bottom third of the league. If the zone command holds, he's a legitimate mid-rotation piece; if hitters learn to sit on what he offers in the zone and stop chasing, the strikeout engine quiets and you're left with a serviceable back-end arm.

reports.name: David Shields
reports.published_report: The K-BB% is the number that matters here, and 21% at A+ is doing real work. David Shields has walked 26 and struck out 101 across 87.7 innings this season, and that combination, not the strikeout rate alone but the command holding the strikeout rate up, is what makes the profile interesting at 19. The translation is sobering: that 10.4 K/9 comes down to 8.0 in MLB-equivalent terms, sitting just below a league-average mark, and the walk rate lands right at it, so the margin for error at higher levels is thin. If the command holds as competition stiffens, he becomes a multi-inning reliever or setup piece; if it slips, the strikeout rate won't carry him and the floor is depth.

reports.name: Demetrio Crisantes
reports.published_report: The bat-to-ball ability is the loud part: a .314/.402/.531 line across AAA & AA & A+ that translates to a K% right at league average and a BB% a tick above it. Demetrio Crisantes is 21 and hitting, which matters, but the ceiling reading here is bench or platoon bat, and the floor isn't much different. The ISO translates to .157, close enough to the .150 MLB average that the power reads as gap-to-gap useful rather than impact, and everything hinges on whether the .363 BABIP is a contact-quality signature or a gifts-from-the-schedule number that softens on the way up. He's cooling in ValuCast's rankings, down 0.36 in score over three days, which fits a profile where the present production is genuine but the gap between floor and ceiling is narrow enough to matter.

What makes this profile uncomfortable is that the barrel rate and the walk rate live in different zip codes from the contact indicators: a 12.0% BB rate that grades well, paired with a whiff rate and chase rate both sitting in the bottom fifth of the league. He's a catcher who projects for 21 home runs in 516 plate appearances, and at the position that's still valuable, but the .647 OPS projection reflects a real ceiling on what happens when a guy barrels the ball at a useful clip and still can't make consistent contact.

reports.name: Eduardo Quintero
reports.published_report: The .424 OBP is the headline, but the translation is where you need to pause. At A+, Eduardo Quintero is drawing 59 walks against 78 strikeouts across 361 plate appearances, and that walk rate translates to 11.6% at the MLB level, a figure that would play comfortably above most big-league lineups. The ISO is where the profile gets honest: .183 in-level translates to .134, which is below what MLB hitters average, meaning the pop shrinks once the level filter goes on. The 36 stolen bases and the contact shape are what give this profile legs, but if the speed doesn't carry as a plus tool in center, what's left is a good-walk, limited-thump skill set that lands him somewhere between a low-end regular and a bench bat.

The strikeout stuff is ordinary, 103 K across those innings translating to an 8.5 K/9, essentially indistinguishable from a league-average MLB arm, so this profile lives or dies on whether the command holds against better hitters. reports.name: Joey Cantillo
reports.published_report: The profile is a paradox: a 30.3% whiff rate sitting next to an 11.2% walk rate, with fastball spin at 1868 rpm. Cantillo misses bats at a legitimate clip, but the fastball is a real problem, sitting 92.1 mph with near-basement spin, which means he can't just throw it past anyone who lays off the secondary stuff. The walk rate is the fulcrum: if he tightens the zone and converts those whiffs into strikeouts without falling behind, a 3.90 xERA foundation can support a mid-rotation innings-eater across a full season, and 156.6 projected innings says Cleveland is already betting on that. If the control doesn't improve, you're paying for a guy who misses barrels (.305 xwOBA is solid) but hands out too many free passes to ever really strand them.

But the power is organizational-depth thin: 3 home runs, a .119 ISO at AAA, and the MLB-equivalent translation lands at .116 ISO against a translated average of .150, which is the shape of a guy whose contact game has to do all the carrying. At A-ball, Taitn Gray has drawn 31 walks against 42 strikeouts in 192 plate appearances, and the discipline translates to a .406 OBP that sits at the 90th percentile among his hitter pool. The swing-and-contact side is softer: his 22% strikeout rate at A ticks up to 25.7% against MLB pitching, which erases some of the plate-discipline gains, and the MLB-equivalent ISO of .132 falls short of where a first baseman needs to be if strikeouts are climbing too. If the eye holds and the bat catches up as an 18-year-old, a low-end everyday regular is the ceiling; if the strikeouts bleed up and the power stalls, the profile thins to reserve.

reports.name: Robert Arias
reports.published_report: The contact-and-walk combination at A-ball is genuinely unusual for a 19-year-old: 14% strikeouts, 15% walks, a .397 OBP across 190 plate appearances in 2026. That discipline translates to a 20.6% K rate and 10.2% BB rate in MLB-equivalent terms, both better than the average big leaguer, which is the part of this profile worth keeping. The power is where the ceiling closes — a .171 ISO at A is fine, but it translates to .127 against big-league pitching, well below the MLB mean, and the 5 home runs in 190 PA don't suggest that gap narrows on its own. If the speed (21 stolen bases at A) plays in center and the bat-to-ball holds as competition rises, there's a path to an everyday-ish role built on contact and baserunning; if the game power never develops, what's left is a bench piece who gets on base.

reports.name: Jacob Melton
reports.published_report: The .391 BABIP is the first thing to squint at, and it's also the first thing that could make this whole read moot. Across 139 AAA plate appearances, Jacob Melton is hitting .272/.377/.500 with 20 stolen bases, and the numbers that survive a BABIP correction are the ones worth watching: 20 walks against 44 strikeouts, with an ISO that translates to .163 in MLB context against a league where the average sits at .15. That strikeout rate translates to 27%, well above the 22% MLB baseline, and at a contact floor that shaky, the ISO needs to hold to keep the profile interesting. If the BABIP normalizes and the strikeouts stay, what's left is a bench outfielder with some speed and fringe power, not nothing, but not a regular.

reports.published_report: The numbers at A+ are loud enough to make you lean in: 1.2 ERA, 0.7 WHIP, 14.3 K/9 against 2.4 BB/9 across 29.7 innings. That's the problem too. Twenty-nine innings is a conversation starter, not a verdict, and the sample is already stale. Translated across AA & A+ & A, the strikeout rate softens to 9.6 K/9 and the walk rate climbs to 3.7, which puts him above a league-average K-BB% but not by a margin that carries a rotation dream. If the stuff translates and the workload builds, there's a back-end starter in there; if it doesn't, you're left with a reliever with good peripherals.
